title: Cursors and Concurrency
description: Process rows one at a time with cursors. Understand how deadlocks occur and learn strategies to prevent and resolve them.

data.text: SQL is built for sets — process thousands of rows at once with a single statement. But sometimes you genuinely need to process rows one at a time, or you need to understand why multiple users stepping on each other's transactions can cause deadlocks.
A cursor is a database object that traverses a result set one row at a time. It has four stages: DECLARE, OPEN, FETCH (in a WHILE loop), and CLOSE + DEALLOCATE.

data.title: Full cursor life cycle
Cursors are slow — avoid them when possible
data.text: A cursor processes one row at a time, which is dramatically slower than a set-based operation. SQL Server's documentation repeatedly recommends rewriting cursor logic as a single UPDATE or SELECT. Use cursors only when you truly need sequential, per-row processing — for example, calling an external API per row.

items: Set-based operations (WHILE + TOP loop to process in batches)
Window functions (ROW_NUMBER, LAG, LEAD) for sequential logic
WHILE loops with a row-number counter
CLR stored procedures for complex per-row processing in .NET

data.text: Deadlocks — when two transactions block each other

A deadlock occurs when two sessions each hold a lock the other needs. Session A locks table X and waits for table Y; session B locks table Y and waits for table X. Neither can proceed — SQL Server steps in and kills one (the 'deadlock victim') to break the cycle.

data.caption: A deadlock: each session holds a lock the other needs, creating a circular wait

data.title: Classic deadlock scenario
Deadlock victim message
data.text: When SQL Server detects a deadlock, it kills one session: 'Transaction (Process ID 65) was deadlocked on lock resources with another process and has been chosen as the deadlock victim. Rerun the transaction.' The application should catch this, wait briefly, and retry.

items: Access tables in the same order in every procedure (if you always update invoices before invoice_items, the circular wait never forms)
Keep transactions short — the shorter the lock duration, the less likely a collision
Use the (READ COMMITTED) snapshot isolation level to reduce locking
Retry logic in the application layer — catch deadlock errors and retry the transaction after a short wait

data.title: Cursors and concurrency takeaways
points: Cursors traverse rows one-by-one; always DEALLOCATE after use to free resources
Cursors are slow — prefer set-based operations or window functions
Deadlocks happen when two sessions create a circular lock dependency
Prevent deadlocks by consistent table access order, short transactions, and retry logic
The deadlock victim gets an error and must be retried by the application
